C
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is the test of choice for identifying chromosomal abnormalities in 22q11.2 deletion. C
Surgical intervention needed for congenital heart defects and cleft palate abnormalities. C
Multidisciplinary teams needed for good prognosis and follow-up. C

background.definition: DiGeorge syndrome is a rare congenital syndrome. Symptoms vary but may include recurrent infections, heart defects, and characteristic facial features. It is also called velocardiofacial syndrome.

list.listitem: DiGeorge syndrome occurs in 1 in 6000 to 6500 births in whites, blacks, and Asians. It occurs in 1 in 3800 births in Hispanics.
Over a 6.5 year period, 3.2 million infants were screened for severe combined immunodeficiency, and 4 patients with complete DiGeorge syndrome who received thymus transplants were identified.
DiGeorge syndrome is the most common diagnosed chromosome deletion syndrome.
It is also the most frequent genetic condition associated with congenital heart defects (after Down syndrome).
It is associated with major psychoses, occurring in up to 25% of adults and adolescents.

Affective disorders, especially anxiety disorder and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are common comorbidities, based on a systematic review of seven studies with 323 affected children. Depressive disorders were also more common, but psychosis was rare in this series and was seen in only two patients.
Approximately 90% of deletions occur de novo.
There is a 50% recurrence risk for each offspring.
About 75% of fetuses affected by DiGeorge syndrome are at risk of congenital heart disease.

DiGeorge syndrome is characterized by signs and symptoms arising from the poor development of the pharyngeal pouches. These embryonic structures develop into the thymus, thyroid, parathyroids, maxilla, mandible, aortic arch, cardiac outflow tract, and external/middle ear.
Deletion 22q11.2 results in defects of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches leading to thymic and parathyroid aplasia and conotruncal heart defects,also manifesting in severe T-cell deficiency.

Within the deletion 22q11.2 lies a critical gene TBX1. TBX1 gene mutation leads to downstream molecular pathway disruption. TBX1, a DNA-binding transcription factor, is expressed in the pharyngeal endoderm, in the paraxial mesodermal core of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th pharyngeal arches in the dorsolateral regions of the aortic sac.

Suspect DiGeorge syndrome in a newborn or infant with hypocalcemia, nasopharyngeal reflux, dysmorphic facial features (ears and nose, hyperterlorlism (present in most Caucasian infants)), absent thymus, and/or congenital heart disease. C

Test any newborn, infant, or child with congenital heart defects for 22q11.2 deletion, as well as any older child or adult with congenital heart defects and/or common features of the 22q11.2 deletion for the 22q11.2 deletion. C
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is the test of choice for identifying chromosomal abnormalities in 22q11.2 deletion. C

list.listitem: Definitive diagnosis: requires reduced numbers of CD3+ T-cells (less than 500/mm3) and 2 of 3 following characteristics: (1) conotruncal cardiac defect (truncus arteriosus, tetratology of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, or aberrant right subclavian), (2) hypocalcemia of greater than 3 weeks' duration that requires therapy, and (3) deletion of chromosome 22q11.2.
Probable diagnosis: requires reduced numbers of CD3+ T-cells (less than 1500/mm3) and a deletion of chromosome 22q11.2.

Possible diagnosis: requires reduced numbers of CD3+ T-cells (less than 1500/mm3) and at least one of the following: (1) cardiac defect, (2) hypocalcemia of greater than 3 weeks' duration that requires therapy, and (3) dysmorphic facies or palatal abnormalities.

Common features of the 22q11 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) include the following: congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia, palate anomalies, velopharyngeal dysfunction and other speech disorders, feeding disorders and growth retardation, otorhinolaryngologic issues, dysmorphic facies, renal anomalies, cognitive or learning disabilities, and behavioral or psychiatric disorders.
Scoliosis occurs in about 50% of affected children. Those with a sagittal shape of the spine are at a higher risk of developing scoliosis (RR 2.6).

An Italian cohort study included 228 patients with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. The median age at diagnosis was 4 months (range 0-37 years); when diagnosed after 2 years, speech and language impairment, developmental delay, and facial features most often led to the diagnosis.

The acronym CATCH-22 has been described to capture the typical features of diGeorge syndrome: Cardiac abnormality, Abnormal facies, Thymic dysplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism, and 22q11 deletion.
Careful examination of the heart, pharynx, and palate is required.
Palate and speech evaluation by an otolaryngologist and speech pathologist may be needed to detect abnormalities.
When clinically suspected order fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) to detect the characteristic chromosomal abnormality. Also order serum calcium to rule out hypocalcemia.
Order echocardiography of heart, subclavian artery, aortic arch to rule out congenital heart abnormalities. If equivocal, consider cardiac MRI.
Test for T-cell markers (i.e. CD3) are used to identify patients with severe immunodeficiency in need of a thymic transplant.
Imaging with videofluoroscopy may be helpful to identify velopharyngeal insufficiency.
Among patients undergoing surgery for congenital heart disease, an elevated mean platelet volume (>10 fL) increased the likelihood of 22q11 deletion.
Suspect DiGeorge syndrome in a newborn or infant with hypocalcemia, nasopharyngeal reflux, typical facial features (ears and nose), absent thymus, and/or congenital heart disease.
If patient has congenital heart disease, then evaluate for 22q11.2 deletion.
If clinically suspected, order FISH, T cell markers (i.e. CD3+), and serum calcium tests.

A guideline from the 22q11.2 Society makes specific recommendations for follow-up testing in adults with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. This includes genetic and prenatal counseling; counseling regarding diet, exercise and vaccinations; relevant vital signs, vision/dental assessment, and relevant blood tests; and targetted assessment of neuropsych, cardiac, endocrine, and other affected systems.
Congenital heart defects require pediatric cardiothoracic surgery consult for possible surgical intervention. C
Consider psychiatric consultation to evaluate and treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and schizophrenic syndromes. C

Psychotic syndromes (schizophrenia, schizotypical trait, or psychotic phenomena) are more common in patients with DiGeorge syndrome. Treat with antipsychotics early with mild psychotic syndromes. Early treatment may prevent progression of prodromal syndromes to schizophrenia in adolescents and young adults. Anxiety disorders are also more common than in the general public (2 to 3 fold).
A systematic review of case reports found 57 individuals with psychotic symptoms treated with clozapine, with 66% having a response reported.

A case report described successful treatment of psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and paranoia) in a patient with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) with riluzole, a drug that reduces glutamatergic neurotransmission.
A small randomized trial of methylphenidate in 34 children and adolescents with DiGeorge syndrome found improved outcomes with treatment compared to placebo.
A trial of S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAMe) found that it was safe but found no evidence of benefit.
Congenital heart defects such as Tetralogy of Fallot or truncus arteriosus may require surgical intervention, including transplant in some cases.
Cleft palate generally requires surgical repair.
Thymus transplant may be considered in patients with athymia.
Consider cognitive behavioral therapy for associated psychiatric problems.
A case series reported improvements in cognition with a neuroplasticity-based computerized cognitive remediation program, but it has not been evaluated in a clinical trial.
Avoid live vaccines due to immunodeficiency.
For the same reason, give only irradiated, cytomegalovirus-negative blood products.
Consider prophylaxis with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for recurrent infections.
Severe immunodeficiency may benefit from gammaglobulin transfusion.
Thymic transplantation or hematopoietic cell transplantation is effective for T-cell deficiency.
Cognition, as measured by IQ, appears to decline over time in children (10 points over 5 years in one study).B
Multidisciplinary teams needed for good prognosis and follow-up. C
Speech and cardiovascular outcomes following surgical correction are encouraging.B
An Italian cohort study with 228 patients found that 92% of patients were alive at 15 years following diagnosis.
During pregnancy, treat and consider personal medical conditions, especially cardiovascular hemodynamic changes.

Prenatal ultrasonography clues for 22q11.2 deletion: polyhydramnios, cleft palate, structural renal abnormalities; less commonly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, myelomeningocele, and congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
